name: Irish English (Hiberno-English, with Dublin focus)
summary: Irish English (Hiberno-English) covers a wide range. This file separates DUBLIN (Local, Mainstream, Advanced/new Dublin) from GENERAL/RURAL Irish English (south-west Cork/Kerry, west, Ulster). Grammar is where Irish English is most distinctive: the 'after' perfect ('hot-news'), habitual 'does be', answering by echoing the verb ('I am.'), 'so I can' tags, 'sure' tags, 'Will I...?', and second-person plurals ye / yis / yous. Round 2 added verified grammar from the Yale Grammatical Diversity Project (after-perfects, embedded-question inversion), a Frontiers in Communication study of Cork/Kerry English (be after, do be), Macquarie Dictionary on 'youse', and more everyday vocabulary from the Hiberno-English article (which cites Dolan's Dictionary of Hiberno-English). It also fixed the FACE vowel: general Irish English tends to a monophthong [eː], Local Dublin to a diphthong. Intonation: Ulster tends to rising statements; the south-west to a 'sing-song' fall. Primary sources (Hickey 2005, 2007; Dolan; the IDEA archive) were NOT opened directly.

grammar.standard: He has just given me cheek.
grammar.dialect: He was after giving me cheek. (after-perfect)
grammar.condition: YGDP: be after + -ing, from the Irish prepositional 'tar éis'; the 'hot-news' perfect used for a recent event the speaker is involved in. Cork example from a study: 'We are after missing the bus.' Present is commoner than past; used with all verb types; rarely negated.
grammar.example_standard: She has just finished her dinner.
grammar.example_dialect: She is after finishing her dinner.

grammar.dialect: He does be working every day. (habitual 'do be')
grammar.condition: Habitual aspect with does be + -ing. Study: Cork/Kerry example 'He does be eating in John B's' (usual habit); speakers aware of standard English increasingly avoid it. Wikipedia lists it for Mayo, Sligo, Wexford, Dublin city centre and Cork, but that section is flagged as uncited. Rural and older flavour.
grammar.example_dialect: He does be working every day.

grammar.dialect: echo the verb: 'I am.', 'He did.', 'They won't.'
grammar.condition: Irish English tends to answer yes/no questions by repeating the verb instead of saying yes or no (Wikipedia, Irish influence).
grammar.example_standard: Are you coming home soon? - Yes.
grammar.example_dialect: Are you coming home soon? - I am.

grammar.dialect: I can speak Irish, so I can. / I am so!
grammar.condition: 'so' as an emphatic tag or a contradiction. Wikipedia: especially in northern dialects (Sligo, Mayo, Ulster).
grammar.example_dialect: I can speak Irish, so I can.

grammar.standard: I was only here five minutes ago!
grammar.condition: 'sure' at the end of a sentence for 'of course / after all'. Munster (south-west) especially (source 1; the passage was partly truncated).
grammar.example_standard: I was only here five minutes ago!
grammar.example_dialect: I was only here five minutes ago, sure!

grammar.condition: Older-sounding contractions of 'it is' (source 1). Traditional, rural or deliberately folksy.

Second-person plural. 'Yous' mainly Dublin and Ulster; 'yiz' in parts of Leinster; 'ye' widely, informal (source 1). Macquarie: 'yez' is the usual Irish spelling and Australian 'youse' came from Irish English (1890s).
grammar.example_standard: Did you all go to see it?
grammar.example_dialect: Did ye all go to see it?

grammar.standard: Shall I make us a cup of tea?
grammar.dialect: Will I make us a cup of tea?
grammar.condition: 'Will' used where British English has 'shall' and American 'should' (source 1).
grammar.example_standard: Shall I make us a cup of tea?
grammar.example_dialect: Will I make us a cup of tea?

grammar.standard: I'm not allowed to go out tonight.
grammar.dialect: I'm not allowed go out tonight.
grammar.condition: 'to' dropped after allowed (source 1; flagged citation needed). Low confidence.
grammar.example_standard: I'm not allowed to go out tonight.
grammar.example_dialect: I'm not allowed go out tonight.

grammar.condition: 'once' in a conditional sense: 'I have no problem laughing at myself once the joke is funny' (source 1).
grammar.example_standard: I have no problem laughing at myself if the joke is funny.
grammar.example_dialect: I have no problem laughing at myself once the joke is funny.

grammar.condition: Old English contraction 'amn't' (source 1). Verified as listed; current frequency not stated.

grammar.standard: I asked if she was coming.
grammar.dialect: I asked her was she coming. (inversion in embedded questions)
grammar.condition: YGDP lists Hiberno English and Belfast English among dialects where the auxiliary can come before the subject in an embedded question (and no 'if/whether'). Frequency not stated; example constructed.
grammar.example_standard: I asked her if she was coming.
grammar.example_dialect: I asked her was she coming.

grammar.condition: Emphatic reflexive for the person present; may sound formal or teasing (source 1). Medium confidence.

pronunciation.rule: Th-stopping outside Ulster: th becomes a dental t or d ('think' -> 'tink', 'this' -> 'dis'). In Dublin it is a Local (working-class) feature, not Mainstream or Advanced; Ulster speakers keep th.
pronunciation.actor_tip: Tongue tip against the back of the top teeth. Only for Local Dublin or rural (non-Ulster) characters.

pronunciation.rule: T-lenition: /t/ between vowels or at word end is a slit fricative (like a weak 's') in most of Ireland outside Ulster. Dublin: Local [t̪] [ʔ] or [h]; Mainstream [ʔ], tap [ɾ] or slit fricative; Advanced Dublin: initial /t, d/ can be affricated [ts] [dz].
pronunciation.actor_tip: 'water' with a soft hissy 't'. Use sparingly; in Advanced Dublin it can sound like 'tsea'.

pronunciation.rule: Rhoticity: r is pronounced everywhere; Local Dublin is weakly rhotic, Advanced Dublin uses retroflex [ɻ].
pronunciation.actor_tip: Pronounce r after vowels in car, hard, girl. Retroflex for Advanced Dublin.

pronunciation.rule: No h-dropping: h is kept; the letter name is 'haitch' /heɪtʃ/.
Yod-dropping after n, l, s ('new', 'sue' = 'noo', 'soo') and yod-coalescence after t, d ('tune' ~ 'choon', 'duty' ~ 'joo-ty').
pronunciation.ipa: /nj lj sj/ -> /n l s/; /tj dj/ -> [tʃ dʒ]

pronunciation.rule: Light (clear) l in most Irish English; Advanced Dublin has darker word-final l; Ulster can have a dark l.
pronunciation.actor_tip: Keep l light with the tongue tip up.

pronunciation.rule: TRAP: [æ] in Local Dublin, [a~ä] in Advanced Dublin; the trap-bath split is partial across Irish English.
pronunciation.actor_tip: Open the mouth a little more for Advanced Dublin.

pronunciation.rule: FACE: general Irish English tends to a monophthong [eː]; Dublin (all kinds) is a diphthong [eɪ~ɛɪ]. Round 1 gave only the Dublin form.
pronunciation.actor_tip: Rural/Western/Cork characters: steady 'ay'. Dubliners: a clear glide.

pronunciation.rule: GOAT: Local Dublin has a wide diphthong [ʌʊ~ʌo]; Advanced a narrower [əʊ]; elsewhere (west) often a monophthong [oː].
pronunciation.actor_tip: Local Dublin 'go' starts with 'uh'; Western 'go' is one pure 'oh'.

pronunciation.rule: PRICE: Local Dublin [əɪ]; Advanced [ɐɪ~ɑɪ]; Ulster front 'ɛɪ'-like before voiceless consonants.
MOUTH: Dublin front and raised [æʊ~ɛʊ~eʊ]; Mainstream [aʊ]; the West has a back start; Ulster fronts the second element.
pronunciation.actor_tip: Start 'now' from the front of the mouth ('neh-oo').

pronunciation.rule: CHOICE: starts lower outside Ulster: Local Dublin [ɑɪ] or [ɒɪ]; Advanced [ɔɪ]/[oɪ].
pronunciation.actor_tip: Open start for Local Dublin ('boy' like 'bah-ee').

pronunciation.rule: THOUGHT/LOT: Local Dublin [ä(ː)] (can merge with LOT); Mainstream [ɒː]; Advanced [oː] closed syllable, [ɔː] open syllable. cot-caught merger is inconsistent.
pronunciation.actor_tip: Do not assume cot = caught for every Irish speaker.

pronunciation.rule: Advanced (new) Dublin merges NORTH/FORCE (horse = hoarse) and NURSE/SQUARE ('fur'/'fair'); Local/conservative speakers keep 'earn' and 'urn' distinct. Advanced Dublin is the likely accent of most Dubliners born after the 1980s (probable, per source 2).
pronunciation.actor_tip: Only for young Dubliners; not for Local characters or rural speakers.

intonation.rule: Ulster English: statements often end on a rising pitch, so they can sound like questions (source 1).
intonation.actor_tip: Use only for Northern Irish characters; a rise at the end of declaratives.

intonation.rule: West and South-West (Cork): a 'sing-song' effect, with pitch rising on stressed long vowels and then falling sharply (source 1).
intonation.actor_tip: Raise pitch on the stressed long vowel and drop it away in the next syllable; use only for Cork/Kerry-type characters.

intonation.rule: Dublin: no pitch pattern found in the opened Dublin English page; do not attach a sing-song to Dublin speakers by default.
intonation.actor_tip: Use the vowel and consonant features first.

common_mistakes: Applying th-stopping to Ulster or to Mainstream/Advanced Dublin characters.
'Top o' the morning', 'begorrah', leprechaun phrases: stage stereotypes.
Putting craic, eejit, feck, banjaxed in every line.
Mixing Local and Advanced Dublin features on one character.
Using a strong American r on every word: Local Dublin is weakly rhotic; Advanced is retroflex.
Using 'after', 'does be', 'yous' and 'so I can' in the same line. Choose one or two per speech.
Giving 'does be' to a young urban character; speakers aware of standard English avoid it (source 5).
A 'sing-song' intonation for all Irish characters. It is a south-west description; Ulster is rising-statements; Dublin is unverified.
Using 'Is it yourself' or 'Tis herself' as general Irish speech; formal, teasing, rare.
generational_notes: Advanced (new) Dublin English is probably the accent of most Dubliners born since the 1980s (source 2), and is said to be becoming the new standard nationwide.
Local Dublin is the traditional working-class accent; its r is weak in the 21st century.
Speakers conscious of standard English increasingly avoid 'does be' (source 5, Cork/Kerry study).
'Whisht', 'childer', 'delph', 'boreen' read as older/rural; 'craic' and 'eejit' are current. No age data in sources.
The Cork/Kerry grammar study used speakers born in the 1920s-1970s (source 5).
conversion_guidelines: Natural spoken film-dialogue English first. Irish flavour comes from rhythm of statement/answer, one or two grammar items, and sparing vocabulary.
Choose the variety first: Dublin (Local / Mainstream / Advanced), or rural (Cork-Kerry, West), or Ulster. Do not mix.
Grammar (one or two per monologue): 'after' perfect for just-happened events; echo-verb answers ('I am.'); 'so I can'; 'Will I...?'; 'ye' for plural you.
Vocabulary: craic, eejit, feck, give out, the messages, press. One or two, only where the scene fits.
Sound notes: Local Dublin th-stopping, MOUTH raised; Advanced Dublin retroflex r and horse=hoarse; rural: monophthong FACE/GOAT.
No eye-dialect; no leprechaun phrases. Ulster: no th-stopping; consider rising statements.
In actor notes name the variety and region.

sources.title: Be after and habitual do be in south-western Hiberno-English (Frontiers in Communication, 2022)
Inversion in embedded questions, Yale Grammatical Diversity Project
Macquarie Dictionary: What're youse doing? (on 'youse', Irish English origin)

open_questions: Primary sources (Hickey 2004, 2005, 2007; Dolan's Dictionary of Hiberno-English; IDEA recordings) were not opened. Wikipedia cites them; vowel IPA should be checked with native recordings.
The Hiberno-English 'To be' (do be) section is flagged uncited on Wikipedia; the regional list (Mayo, Sligo, Wexford, Dublin city centre, Cork) is unverified.
'Grand', 'gas', 'sure look', 'yer man', 'gobshite', 'gaff' and 'slagging' were not found in the opened text; omitted.
Dublin intonation: not described in the opened Dublin article. Derry (rising) and Galway (falling) studies appeared in search results only (not opened).
Is 'Is it yourself' / 'Tis herself' used by younger speakers? Unknown.
Embedded-question inversion: YGDP lists Hiberno English but gives no frequency; example is constructed.
Word ages (whisht, childer, delph, jackeen, mot) are coaching judgement; sources give no age.
'Sure' tag: the Wikipedia passage was truncated; check Munster use.
Ulster English needs its own file (Ulster Scots, rising declaratives, different vowels).

sub_regions.name: 더블린: Local vs Mainstream vs Advanced
sub_regions.note: Local = 전통 노동계층(th-stopping, [t̪]/[ʔ]/[h], 넓은 GOAT), Mainstream = 중산층, Advanced = 1980년대 이후 출생 다수의 새 억양(horse=hoarse, 레트로플렉스 r). 한 인물에 섞지 마세요(출처 2).

sub_regions.name: 더블린 vs 시골
sub_regions.note: 'does be'는 시골과 더블린 시내·코크 도시에서 보고되지만 위키 해당 절은 출처 미표기. 'youse'는 더블린·얼스터, 'yiz'는 레인스터 일부(출처 1). 시골 화자일수록 whisht/childer 등 옛 어휘가 어울림(감).

sub_regions.name: 얼스터(북아일랜드)
sub_regions.note: th-stopping 없음, 평서문 끝 상승 억양, GOOSE-FOOT 병합 경향, 'so' 태그가 많음(출처 1). 별도 파일 필요.

sub_regions.name: 서부·남서부(코크·케리)
sub_regions.note: MOUTH가 뒤쪽, GOAT는 단모음 유지, 'sing-song' 억양, 'sure' 태그(먼스터). be after, do be 연구 지역(출처 1, 5).

sub_regions.name: 표준(supraregional) 아일랜드 영어
sub_regions.note: 교육받은 중산·상류층의 전국 억양. 영국 RP와 일부 닮았지만 아일랜드적 특징이 남음(출처 1).

confidence_detail: medium-high for after-perfect, do be and 'youse' (academic pages opened); medium for Dublin vowel values (Wikipedia citing Hickey); medium-low for general vocabulary and regional labels (Wikipedia only); low for Dublin intonation (none found).
